slides.title: Session transport
slides.subtitle: Send every request with a fresh Session JWT, and know when not to send it
slides.notes: Once a Session exists, the agent calls the company's APIs and conversations in it, signed in with an access token or signed out without one. This example shows the HTTP client that does that safely: a fresh Session JWT on every attempt, one restart on invalid_session, and no redirects.

slides.title: Why a transport of its own
slides.statement: A valid Session JWT is **only half** of the job. The other half is **where and when** it is sent.
slides.notes: Signing a correct Session JWT is not enough. The transport has to get a new one for each attempt, refuse a redirect rather than resend the token to another URL, and stop callers from swapping in their own credentials.

slides.title: Who takes part
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR M["Model"] subgraph HOST["Your host, trusted"] direction TB T["Agent tool
opaque references"] --> H["Session HTTP client
owns the headers"] H -- "sign this request" --> P["Reactor Session signer
holds the delegated key"] end subgraph CO["Company"] direction TB C["Company API"] end HOST -- "request, Poppy-Session, Bearer token" --> CO HOST -. "API result only" .-> M
slides.caption: The tool holds a reference, the client holds the headers, the signer holds the key; the model gets the result.
slides.notes: Read the host from the top. The agent tool asks for a company resource and holds only opaque references. The Session HTTP client, SessionHttpClient in Python and SessionFetchClient in TypeScript, owns the Authorization and Poppy-Session headers. It asks the Reactor Session signer for a Session JWT bound to the method, the target and the token hash, without ever seeing the key. Only the request, the access token and the Session JWT cross to the company API. Off to the side, the model: it gets the API result, never an access token, a Session JWT or a key.

slides.title: A request that restarts the Session

items.title: Sign
items.detail: JWT 1 for GET /orders and the token hash

items.title: Restart once
items.detail: A new Session, JWT 2 for the same request: 200

slides.notes: The first attempt is refused with invalid_session: the Session failed a check, or it has ended. The client starts a new Session in its place, signs a second JWT for the same request, and sends it again. The tool gets the API result, with no token or Session JWT in it.

slides.title: The redirect is refused
slides.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Agent tool
  participant H as Session client
  participant C as Company API
  A->>H: GET orders again
  H->>C: Token + JWT 3
  C-->>H: 307 to /orders/current
  H-->>A: redirect_refused
slides.notes: On the second call the company answers with a redirect. The client does not follow it: under draft 0.3 no token, Session JWT, assertion or body goes to the URL a protocol endpoint redirects to. The tool gets redirect_refused, and nothing reaches the new URL.

slides.title: Enforced boundaries
items: HTTPS resource URLs only, with no embedded credentials
`Authorization`, `Poppy-Session` and the signature headers are host-owned: callers cannot set them
A fresh Session JWT for every attempt, including the resend
Request bodies are replayable values, not streams
slides.notes: These are the rules the client enforces. Notice the last one: because a restart resends the body, bodies are values that can be sent twice, not streams that can be read once.

slides.title: Each answer, decided
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR S["Send with
a fresh Session JWT"] --> Q{"Company answers"} Q -- "200" --> R["Result to the tool
no token or JWT"] Q -- "307 redirect" --> X["redirect_refused
nothing sent on"] Q -- "first invalid_session" --> F["A new Session"] F --> S Q -- "second invalid_session" --> Y["Back to the caller"]
slides.caption: Every attempt gets its own Session JWT, one restart at most, and a redirect is never followed.
slides.notes: Start at the left: every attempt goes out with a fresh Session JWT. A 200 goes back to the tool with no token or JWT in it. A redirect stops right there with redirect_refused, and nothing is sent to the new URL. An invalid_session starts a new Session once, and the request is sent again in it; a second one in a row goes back to the caller. Because a restart resends the body, request bodies are replayable values, not streams.

slides.title: MCP has its own client
slides.statement: An MCP token is issued for **one server's URL**, asked for with `resource`, and works **only there**.
slides.notes: A refresh with resource set to the server's url gets the token: token_for_mcp in Python, tokenForMcp in TypeScript. There is no Token Exchange any more. McpClient sends it through McpSessionAuth, which adds the Session header and a plain Bearer token, and refuses any other URL before a request is sent. So an MCP token never reaches the company's API.

slides.title: Run it yourself
slides.cta: The Pydantic AI and Agent Runtimes examples send a request through a Session restart, then meet a refused redirect
slides.notes: Both examples run the same two calls: one that succeeds after a restart, and one that stops at a redirect. Upstream's Sessions section has the rules in full.
